items.stem: Distinguish between incomplete combustion and complete combustion.
items.answer: Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O and releases maximum energy; incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives CO and/or C as well, and releases less energy.
items.markingKey: Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O and releases maximum energy; incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives CO and/or C as well, and releases less energy. items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why incomplete combustion releases less energy than complete combustion.
items.answer: Carbon is only partly oxidised (to CO or C), so fewer strong C=O bonds are formed in CO₂ and less energy is released overall. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Carbon is only partly oxidised (to CO or C), so fewer strong C=O bonds are formed in CO₂ and less energy is released overall. items.stem: Isabel writes: "Fuels with the highest enthalpy of combustion per mole are always the best fuels for cars." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "complete combustion"?

Burning a fuel in a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water
A fuel produced from recently living biomass, such as bioethanol or biodiesel; considered renewable
Burning a fuel in a plentiful supply of oxygen, so that carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen to water
items.answer: Burning a fuel in a plentiful supply of oxygen, so that carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen to water
items.markingKey: D. "complete combustion" is burning a fuel in a plentiful supply of oxygen, so that carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen to water.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Natural gas is a suitable “bridge fuel” in the transition from coal to renewables."
items.answer: It reduces emissions relative to coal only if methane leakage is minimised and it is phased out on a clear timetable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about half the CO₂ per kWh of coal; flexible power generation backing up renewables. the anode, where hydrogen is supplied
items.answer: the anode, where hydrogen is supplied
items.markingKey: D. An Ox, Red Cat.

items.stem: Which fuel produces the least CO₂ per kJ of energy released?
items.answer: methane
items.markingKey: C. Highest H:C ratio.

items.stem: Which is produced when biodiesel is made by transesterification?
items.answer: glycerol
items.markingKey: B. Triglyceride + 3CH₃OH → 3 methyl esters + glycerol.

items.stem: Explain why fuel cells are more efficient than combustion engines for converting chemical energy into useful work.
items.answer: They convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy without first producing heat, so they are not limited by the heat-engine (Carnot) efficiency; less energy is wasted as heat.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy without first producing heat, so they are not limited by the heat-engine (Carnot) efficiency; less energy is wasted as heat. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Calculate the minimum mass of ethanol (C₂H₅OH, ΔHc = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹) that must be burned to release 2.50 × 10⁵ kJ of energy.

Compare pentane (ΔHc = −3509 kJ mol⁻¹) and hexane (ΔHc = −4163 kJ mol⁻¹) by calculating the mass of CO₂ produced per MJ of energy released. Deduce which has the lower carbon footprint per unit energy.
items.answer: pentane 62.7 g MJ⁻¹; hexane 63.4 g MJ⁻¹; pentane
items.markingKey: mol CO₂ per mol fuel from formula (M1); 62.7 and 63.4 g CO₂ per MJ (A1 A1); pentane lower (A1).

items.stem: Calculate the mass of hydrogen needed by a fuel cell of efficiency 50 % to supply 5000 kJ of electrical energy (ΔHc(H₂) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: energy needed from reaction = 5000/0.5 = 10000 kJ (M1); n = /286 = 35.0 mol (M1); m = 70.6 g (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Fuels with the highest enthalpy of combustion per mole are always the best fuels for cars." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Practical choice depends on specific energy, energy density, cost, safety, emissions and availability; per-mole values favour large molecules but per-mass values may not.
items.markingKey: Practical choice depends on specific energy, energy density, cost, safety, emissions and availability; per-mole values favour large molecules but per-mass values may not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Biofuels produce no carbon dioxide when burned." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biofuels release CO₂ on combustion; the claimed benefit is that a similar amount was recently absorbed during plant growth.
items.markingKey: Biofuels release CO₂ on combustion; the claimed benefit is that a similar amount was recently absorbed during plant growth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For an acidic methanol fuel cell, write the half-equations at the anode and cathode and the overall equation. State the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
items.answer: anode: CH₃OH + H₂O → CO₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻; cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O; overall: 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O; electrons flow from anode to cathode
items.markingKey: anode (oxidation) CH₃OH + H₂O → CO₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻ (1); cathode (reduction) O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (1); overall 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O (1); electrons anode → cathode (1).

items.stem: What energy is released when 10.0 g of pentane is burned completely, given ΔHc = −3509 kJ mol⁻¹?
items.answer: 486 kJ

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Natural gas is a suitable “bridge fuel” in the transition from coal to renewables."
items.answer: It reduces emissions relative to coal only if methane leakage is minimised and it is phased out on a clear timetable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about half the CO₂ per kWh of coal; flexible power generation backing up renewables. Arguments against: methane leakage is a potent greenhouse gas (about 80 × CO₂ over 20 years); locks in fossil infrastructure; still a non-renewable fossil fuel. Supported judgement: It reduces emissions relative to coal only if methane leakage is minimised and it is phased out on a clear timetable.

items.stem: A hydrogen fuel cell is supplied with 6 kg of hydrogen and operates at 60 % efficiency for 2 hour(s). (a) Write the overall equation. (b) Calculate the electrical energy produced. (c) Calculate the average power output in kW. (d) State and explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using hydrogen as a fuel.
items.markingKey: (a) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (A1). (b) n = 2970 mol; × 286 × 0.6 = 5.10 × 10⁵ kJ (M1 A1). (c) P = E/t = 70.8 kW (A1). (d) e.g. only water produced / high specific energy; storage and production from fossil fuels (R1).

items.stem: Compare propan-1-ol (ΔHc = −2021 kJ mol⁻¹, density 0.803 g cm⁻³) and ethanol (ΔHc = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹, density 0.789 g cm⁻³) as fuels. (a) Calculate the specific energy and energy density of each. (b) Deduce which fuel would allow a car with a 50 dm³ tank to travel further. (c) Discuss one other factor that should be considered.
items.answer: (a) propan-1-ol: 33.6 kJ g⁻¹, 27000 kJ dm⁻³; ethanol: 29.7 kJ g⁻¹, 23400 kJ dm⁻³; (b) propan-1-ol
items.markingKey: (a) specific energies 33.6 and 29.7 kJ g⁻¹ (A1 A1); energy densities 27000 and 23400 kJ dm⁻³ (A1). (b) propan-1-ol – higher energy per volume (R1). (c) e.g. CO₂ per kJ, renewable source, cost, toxicity, volatility (R1).

items.stem: "Replacing petrol with bioethanol will solve the problem of climate change from transport." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Bioethanol can reduce emissions but cannot alone solve the problem; electrification, efficiency and reduced demand are also needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: renewable, reduces fossil carbon emissions; can be blended with petrol in existing cars. Arguments against: farming and processing still emit CO₂ and N₂O; land use competes with food and drives deforestation; lower energy density means more fuel needed. Supported judgement: Bioethanol can reduce emissions but cannot alone solve the problem; electrification, efficiency and reduced demand are also needed. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Why is carbon monoxide toxic?
options: It binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in the blood.
items.answer: It binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in the blood.
items.markingKey: B. Carboxyhaemoglobin.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A fuel (coal, crude oil, natural gas) formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms; non-renewable"?
items.answer: fossil fuel
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of fossil fuel.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A fuel cell in which hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen reduced at the cathode, with water as the only product"?
items.answer: hydrogen fuel cell
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of hydrogen fuel cell.

items.stem: Briefly explain why alcohols release less energy per mole than alkanes with the same number of carbon atoms.
items.answer: Alcohols are already partially oxidised (contain an O atom); fewer bonds to oxygen are formed on combustion, so less energy is released.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Alcohols are already partially oxidised (contain an O atom); fewer bonds to oxygen are formed on combustion, so less energy is released. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between fossil fuels and biofuels.
items.answer: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years and are finite, releasing ancient carbon; biofuels come from recent biomass, are renewable and recycle atmospheric carbon (in principle carbon neutral).
items.markingKey: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years and are finite, releasing ancient carbon; biofuels come from recent biomass, are renewable and recycle atmospheric carbon (in principle carbon neutral). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Hydrogen fuel cells produce electricity by burning hydrogen." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: There is no combustion: hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically at the anode and electrons flow through the external circuit.
items.markingKey: There is no combustion: hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically at the anode and electrons flow through the external circuit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between incomplete combustion and complete combustion.
items.answer: Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O and releases maximum energy; incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives CO and/or C as well, and releases less energy.
items.markingKey: Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O and releases maximum energy; incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives CO and/or C as well, and releases less energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the combustion of fossil fuels contributes to climate change.
items.answer: Burning releases CO₂ that had been locked away for millions of years; increased atmospheric CO₂ absorbs more of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth, enhancing the greenhouse effect and raising average temperatures.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Burning releases CO₂ that had been locked away for millions of years; increased atmospheric CO₂ absorbs more of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth, enhancing the greenhouse effect and raising average temperatures. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a primary cell and a fuel cell.
items.answer: A fuel cell has reactants supplied continuously and can operate indefinitely; a primary cell contains a fixed amount of reactants and stops when they are used up, and cannot be recharged.
items.markingKey: A fuel cell has reactants supplied continuously and can operate indefinitely; a primary cell contains a fixed amount of reactants and stops when they are used up, and cannot be recharged. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: What energy is released when 5.00 g of benzene is burned completely, given ΔHc = −3268 kJ mol⁻¹?
items.answer: 209 kJ

items.stem: "Hydrogen fuel cells are the best option for future transport." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Promising for heavy transport, but batteries currently suit cars better; green hydrogen production is the key condition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: only water emitted at point of use; fast refuelling and long range compared with batteries; high efficiency. Arguments against: hydrogen storage requires high pressure or very low temperature; most hydrogen comes from fossil fuels; catalysts use expensive platinum; infrastructure is limited. Supported judgement: Promising for heavy transport, but batteries currently suit cars better; green hydrogen production is the key condition. items.stem: "Energy density is more important than specific energy when choosing a fuel for vehicles." Discuss.
items.answer: For road vehicles energy density is critical, for aircraft both matter; the best choice balances energy, safety, cost and environmental impact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fuel tanks have limited volume; liquid fuels like petrol and diesel have high energy density. Arguments against: mass matters for aircraft and rockets; specific energy and safety both affect range and efficiency; cost and emissions are major factors. Supported judgement: For road vehicles energy density is critical, for aircraft both matter; the best choice balances energy, safety, cost and environmental impact.
